The silver-cheeked toadfish Lagocephalus sceleratus is a large-bodied tetraodontid that has become a prominent invasive species in the Mediterranean basin. Field surveys in Levantine coastal waters have documented that females attain a total length of 110 centimeters [Li = 110 centimeters] at the upper end of their growth trajectory, a size that corresponds to an ultimate wet weight of 9700 grams [Wwi = 9700 grams]. These maximum dimensions place this species among the largest members of its genus, with individuals inhabiting warmer sectors of their range often reaching greater asymptotic sizes than those from cooler, marginal environments. Growth increments slow markedly after the onset of sexual maturation, with most somatic expansion occurring before the reproductive phase begins. The species displays a characteristic pufferfish body plan, with a robust, somewhat elongated trunk and a large, blunt head. Their skin lacks scales but is covered in small, embedded spinules that provide a degree of protection against predators. The silvery flanks and dark, mottled dorsal surface give the fish its common name and provide effective countershading in the pelagic and coastal habitats it frequents.

Reproductive biology data from eastern Mediterranean populations indicate that puberty, defined as the attainment of gonadal maturity, occurs when individuals reach a total length of 43.3 centimeters [Lp = 43.3 centimeters]. This length threshold is typically reached within the first two to three years of life under prevailing thermal regimes. Histological examination of dissected gonads has confirmed that oocyte development begins once this size is attained, marking a clear transition from the juvenile to the adult phase. The length at puberty shows relatively low variability across the region, suggesting a strong genetic or physiological constraint on the timing of reproductive maturation. After reaching this size, the fish begin to allocate resources toward gamete production, though first successful spawning may lag behind the onset of gonadal activity by several months depending on local environmental conditions. Tag-recapture studies have helped refine growth models for this species, enabling precise estimation of the age-length relationship.

Spawning aggregations of L. sceleratus have been observed during the late spring and summer months when sea surface temperatures are elevated. At a stable water temperature of 27.3 °C [T = 27.3 °C], the gonadosomatic index (GSI) averaged 11% [GSI = 11%]. Coincident measurements of relative fecundity reveal a value of 780.8 eggs per gram of female body mass, a figure that contributes to the species' high reproductive output. This reproductive strategy allows the species to quickly colonize new habitats, which is a key factor in its invasive success.

Early life history stages of the silver-cheeked toadfish begin with the fertilised ovum, which has a mean diameter of 0.64 millimeters. From this diameter, the calculated wet weight at birth is estimated at 0.00014 grams [Wwb = 0.00014 grams], reflecting the small, transparent eggs typical of pelagic spawners. Yolk-sac larvae emerge after a brief incubation period, during which the embryo relies entirely on its endogenous yolk reserves. Mortality during the early larval stages is high, a common feature among marine teleosts that produce large numbers of small offspring. The transition to exogenous feeding occurs when the mouth becomes functional and the yolk reserves are substantially depleted, at which point the tiny larvae begin to capture planktonic prey. The low individual birth mass is offset by the high fecundity of adults, ensuring that at least some offspring survive the intense predation pressure characteristic of the pelagic environment. Rearing experiments conducted at stable temperatures have helped quantify the relationship between egg size and larval survival.

Longevity data for L. sceleratus suggest a maximum lifespan of about 7 years [am = about 7 years] at 27.3 °C [T = 27.3 °C], a duration that is consistent with its moderately fast life-history strategy. This lifespan estimate is derived from otolith readings of the oldest individuals sampled in the eastern Mediterranean. The age structure of wild populations typically shows a high proportion of young individuals, indicating sustained recruitment and relatively high adult mortality rates after the fifth year. The species does not exhibit the extreme longevity seen in some deep-water tetraodontids, instead following a pattern of rapid early growth, early maturity, and an intermediate adult lifespan. Temperature is a critical factor influencing ageing in ectotherms, and the consistent thermal environment of 27.3 °C [T = 27.3 °C] is associated with a metabolic rate that drives the observed rate of senescence. Comparative data from other members of the family Tetraodontidae indicate that lifespan is inversely correlated with ambient temperature, a pattern that holds for this species as well.
